title: Password reset / recovery
summary: Forgot-password: Host-poisoned mail, enumeration, token reuse, cross-account bind, MFA wipe, and reset flooding.

groups.title: Reset mail
groups.summary: How the link is built and whether the flow discloses accounts.

checks.title: Host-poisoned reset link
checks.why: The reset email is built from Host or a forwarding header, so the token is delivered to an attacker origin.
checks.validate: The mail contains a working token URL whose host is one you control. Use a disposable account and inbox.

variants.name: Arbitrary Host
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: The email must still point at the canonical origin.
variants.why: A poisoned Host in the reset link redirects the reset request to an attacker host.

variants.name: X-Forwarded-Host
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: Same check. Also try X-Forwarded-Proto: http and Forwarded: host=evil.example.
variants.why: An unauthenticated forwarding header can override the authority used to build the reset URL.

variants.name: Duplicate Host
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: Edge and app must agree. The mail host is the evidence, not the HTTP response.
variants.why: Front-end/back-end disagreement on duplicate Host values can poison the generated link.

checks.title: Reset account enumeration
checks.why: Forgot-password tells you which addresses exist.
checks.validate: Responses distinguish existing from non-existing accounts consistently.

variants.name: Known vs unknown address
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=known.user%40example.com
variants.expect: Compare with no.such.user@example.com. Diff status, body, JSON code, and timing.
variants.why: A different response for a registered address enumerates accounts.

variants.name: Username-based reset
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"admin"}
variants.expect: Same comparison on a known vs invented username.
variants.why: A reset flow keyed on username leaks account existence when the token is emailed.

groups.title: Token and completion
groups.summary: Entropy, reuse, account bind, MFA survival, and bounded mail flooding.

checks.title: Reset token properties
checks.why: Predictable, reusable, or raced tokens take over the inbox-holder's account.
checks.validate: The same token works twice, for another account, or is guessable from a small sample.

variants.name: Reuse after first use
variants.payload: Request a reset, complete it, then replay the same URL.
variants.expect: Second use must fail. Also try two parallel completions of the same token.
variants.why: A reset token that works twice is not consumed.

variants.name: Token in Referer
variants.payload: Open the reset link, then click any third-party resource on the page and inspect Referer.
variants.expect: The token must not leave the origin.
variants.why: A token leaked through Referer is reusable.

variants.name: Short or sequential token
variants.payload: Request three resets for your account and compare the tokens.
variants.expect: Must look random (long hex/base64url). Sequential integers or short numeric OTPs need extra rate limits.
variants.why: A short or sequential token is guessable and can be brute-forced.

checks.title: Reset bound to the requested account
checks.why: The completion request accepts a different user id, or the token is not tied to the account that requested it.
checks.validate: The password that changes is not the account that requested the reset.

variants.name: Swap user id on complete
variants.payload:
POST /reset-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"token":"<token-for-A>","user_id":2,"password":"NewPass1!"}
variants.expect: Must change A, not B. Also try email=b@example.com alongside A's token.
variants.why: Submitting a different user id at completion resets a different account.

variants.name: Cross-account token
variants.payload: Request resets for A and B. Complete B's form with A's token.
variants.expect: Must fail. A success is account takeover.
variants.why: A token generated for one account completing for another is a binding failure.

checks.title: MFA survives password recovery
checks.why: Completing reset silently drops MFA or recovery codes, so inbox access becomes full account access.
checks.validate: After reset, MFA is still required (or the product documents that recovery is a full factor reset and notifies the user).

variants.name: Login after reset
variants.payload: Reset the password on an MFA-enrolled test account, then log in with the new password only.
variants.expect: Must still prompt for the second factor unless the product explicitly treats reset as factor recovery.
variants.why: MFA must survive a password reset; a fresh login that skips it is the gap.

variants.name: Recovery-code wipe
variants.payload: After reset, try a previously generated recovery code and look for a security-event mail.
variants.expect: Codes should still work or be rotated with a notification — silent wipe plus no MFA is the worst case.
variants.why: A reset that wipes recovery codes can be turned into a DoS against MFA enrollment.

checks.title: Reset mail flooding
checks.why: Unbounded reset mail is a mailbox DoS and a token-oracle.
checks.validate: A bounded burst is throttled. Do not flood a real user; use your test account.

variants.name: Five resets, one account
variants.expect: Captcha, backoff, or 429. If five mails arrive immediately, record the count and stop.
variants.why: A small burst on one account tests reset-mail flooding without spamming.

variants.name: Cross-account spray (do not)
variants.payload: Do not spray reset at other people. If the control is per-IP only, note the gap without demonstrating it against anyone else.
variants.expect: Per-account limits matter more than per-IP.
variants.why: Documented here as out-of-scope; spraying many accounts is abusive and not performed.
